 opened the current week as one of the most closely watched names across American banking after the group delivered third-quarter earnings that topped the prior year. The release landed during the busiest stretch of the quarterly calendar, when the biggest American banks post results within days of one another. For JPMorgan Chase, the headline message was broad strength, as trading, advisory work, lending and consumer banking each added to the top line rather than leaning on any single engine to carry the quarter. Management framed the result against a steadying American economy, pointing to continued spending by families as a force that kept activity firm even amid shifting borrowing costs. That framing set the tone for an update that market participants read as confirmation the group was still gaining ground across its many lines of work. Attention centered on how widely the gains were spread. Rather than relying on a single division, JPMorgan Chase posted advances across markets, advisory work, lending and card activity, a pattern market participants tend to read as a sign of durable momentum rather than a one-off swing tied to a single busy desk. The group also raised its full-year guidance for net interest earnings, a measure that tracks the gap between what the bank earns on loans and securities and what it pays on deposits and borrowings. Lifting that guidance partway through the year signaled management confidence that lending margins were staying firm as the American rate environment shifted. The markets business was a standout. Total trading revenue advanced by a double-digit margin from a year earlier, led by equities, where revenue surged by roughly half as desks handling stocks and derivatives captured heavy client flow through a volatile stretch for American shares. Rates and credit trading told a quieter story, easing modestly against a strong comparison in the prior year. Even so, the combined markets result underscored how large American banks have leaned on trading desks to offset softer stretches elsewhere, turning market volatility into a steady source of fee generation across the quarter. The strength also reflected years of steady spending on trading systems and data platforms, which let the group handle surges in client activity without strain. That operational depth has become a defining feature of how JPMorgan Chase competes against both traditional rivals and newer entrants in markets. Advisory and capital-markets fees climbed by a double-digit margin, helped mainly by stronger advisory work on corporate deals. A reviving appetite for mergers and share sales fed through to the division, which had spent earlier stretches contending with a quieter dealmaking backdrop across the American market. Equity underwriting added to the advance as more companies tapped public markets to raise capital. JPMorgan Chase held a leading share of global fees for the year, reinforcing the group's standing among the handful of American firms that dominate large cross-border transactions and corporate capital raising. The rebound mattered because fee-based advisory work carries high margins and tends to recover quickly once confidence comes back to boardrooms. A busier pipeline of announced deals offered an early sign that corporate activity was thawing after a cautious spell, a shift with read-through for the wider sector. The consumer and community banking arm, the part of JPMorgan Chase that most American families interact with directly, posted higher revenue and net earnings. Card services and auto lending advanced, card spending volumes rose, and the group added several hundred thousand net new checking accounts over the quarter. That steady family engagement matters because it anchors the deposit base that funds the rest of the bank. Management pointed to resilient consumer spending as a reason the broader American economy continued to stay firm, even as families navigated shifting borrowing costs and a mixed labor backdrop. Capital is pouring into the sport, which has become a strategic asset class with a flourishing investment ecosystem. The 2026–2027 football season in Europe recently kicked off — and investors are hoping to score big. This is especially true as the “beautiful game” has evolved beyond a traditional spectator sport and into an attractive asset class. Major football clubs in Europe are highly sought after because they offer various opportunities for value creation, thanks to their engaged consumer base and lucrative media rights. According to Deloitte, the European football market generated a record €40.2 billion in revenue over the 2024/2025 season, crossing the €40 billion threshold for the first time. Additionally, Football Benchmark reports that the aggregate enterprise value of Europe’s top 32 football clubs has nearly tripled since 2016, significantly outpacing general inflation and traditional financial indices. Today, investors are pouring capital into European football through various avenues, from M&A to structured equity and debt financing. What are the key investment trends to watch, and how is the market maturing? The rise of multi-club ownership in European football Multi-club ownership (MCO) occurs when a single investor holds controlling or minority stakes in multiple football clubs across different leagues. It is one of the most significant investment trends in European football today, offering advantages such as: While MCO can create a conflict of interest, it is managed through strict rules — for instance, governing bodies like the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) enforce rules stating that two clubs controlled by the same owner cannot play in the same tournament. Currently, over 120 top-division football clubs in Europe — around 16% of the total — are part of an MCO network. This includes almost half of those in the “Big Five” leagues, namely: Prominent examples include RB Leipzig and FC Red Bull Salzburg (part of the Red Bull franchise), as well as Manchester City FC and Girona FC (under City Football Group). In December 2024, Everton FC became part of an MCO portfolio when it was acquired by privately held consortium The Friedkin Group, which also owns AS Roma and AS Cannes. J.P. Morgan facilitated the process, providing an initial bilateral credit facility of £130 million to fund the acquisition. Thereafter, the firm raised £350 million of debt to help refinance Everton FC’s new stadium, which opened in February 2025 — a key milestone under the club’s new ownership. The growing role of private capital and private wealth Like The Friedkin Group, private capital players are increasingly acquiring stakes in European football clubs, attracted by under-monetized commercial revenues and rising franchise valuations. More than a third of clubs in Europe’s “Big Five” leagues now have backing from private equity, venture capital or private credit firms. In August 2022, private equity firm RedBird Capital Partners purchased AC Milan from hedge fund Elliott Management for €1.2 billion, with the aim of expanding the club’s commercial presence globally. J.P. Morgan advised AC Milan on the deal, which marked the largest ever football transaction in Italy. Ultra-high-net-worth individuals are also headlining major buyouts. Take, for instance, British businessman Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s purchase of a 25% stake in Manchester United in December 2023, which was the largest ever transaction in the EMEA sporting world. J.P. Morgan advised Sir Ratcliffe on the roughly £1.25 billion deal. The firm was also instrumental in advising Italian-American businessman Rocco Commisso, the former chairman of Mediacom, in his acquisition of Serie A club ACF Fiorentina back in 2019. Transactions such as these are a testament to J.P. Morgan’s holistic sports investment banking ecosystem, with the firm’s Private Bank servicing high-net-worth individuals interested in investing in sports and the Corporate and Investment Bank facilitating the deals. “By partnering across the firm, we’re able to drive successful outcomes and deliver exceptional value for our clients,” said Eric Menell, global co-head of Sports Investment Banking at J.P. Morgan. “By partnering across the firm, we’re able to drive successful outcomes and deliver exceptional value for our clients.” Global Co-Head of Sports Investment Banking, J.P. Morgan Stadium redevelopment has become a defining capital investment theme in European football. Many clubs are modernizing aging infrastructure to meet stricter UEFA standards. Some are also reimagining stadiums as mixed-use entertainment platforms that can host non-sporting events — increasing both project complexity and the scale of financing. At the same time, investor interest in sports infrastructure assets such as stadiums and arenas has increased dramatically as valuations have risen. “Part of that is due to the value of live content, which consumers are gravitating toward,” said Tim Self, head of Public Finance and Infrastructure Direct Lending at J.P. Morgan. “Also, unlike in the U.S., where new franchises are still being formed as certain leagues expand into new markets, there’s effectively a fixed supply of sports assets in Europe. As more wealth is created, there’s a lot of money chasing a limited number of top-tier sports assets — and that’s driving valuations to ever higher levels.” J.P. Morgan has structured numerous stadium financings in Europe, supporting clients with capital and arranging syndication across both loan and bond markets. The firm is the leading global arranger and agent for sports and entertainment infrastructure transactions, and has $3.5 billion in capital currently committed for stadium, arena and related infrastructure debt financings globally. A case in point is Real Madrid CF’s five-year renovation of its Santiago Bernabéu stadium, which transformed the iconic venue into a state-of-the-art entertainment hub complete with a retractable grass pitch. J.P. Morgan was deeply involved throughout the project’s lifecycle — from navigating court challenges to structuring financing terms. The firm served as sole placement agent for all four financing rounds, securing multiple ‘A’ category ratings and raising a total of €1.5 billion. In the same vein, FC Barcelona is currently refurbishing its Camp Nou stadium, with works expected to be completed by 2028. The new design is expected to increase the stadium’s capacity from 99,000 to more than 105,000 spectators, as well as add a VIP ring and a sweeping panoramic screen. J.P. Morgan spearheaded the $1.6 billion capital raise, acting as financing bank, structuring agent and placement agent. Both the Santiago Bernabéu and Camp Nou are slated to host matches during the 2030 FIFA World Cup, showcasing the outcomes of these transactions on a global stage. “As more wealth is created, there’s a lot of money chasing a limited number of top-tier sports assets — and that’s driving valuations to ever higher levels.” Head of Public Finance and Infrastructure Direct Lending, J.P. Morgan From blockbuster deals to behind-the-scenes transactions While mega-deals continue to dominate headlines, investors are also supporting European football clubs behind the scenes. “Football clubs today sit on a broad range of valuable but often illiquid assets,” said Taoufik Bounhar, global head of Credit Solutions Trading at J.P. Morgan. “Our Global Credit Solutions Trading team works alongside our Banking, Public Finance and Private Bank partners to deliver bespoke financing and liquidity solutions, helping clubs and owners unlock value from player transfer-related cash flows, as well as media, sponsorship and other contractual receivables. We also offer selected opportunities that we underwrite to our Alternative Credit investors — either through outright participation or synthetic risk-transfer structures — creating efficient capital solutions for clubs while providing investors access to differentiated credit investment opportunities.” In addition, J.P. Morgan offers European football clubs other solutions like debt structuring. For instance, following Chelsea FC’s takeover in 2022, J.P. Morgan structured an £800 million debt facility for the club’s new owners, investment consortium BlueCo. The package included a £500 million term loan dedicated to infrastructure and operational investments, and a £300 million revolving credit facility for working capital. More recently, Sporting Clube de Portugal (also known as Sporting Lisbon) teamed up with J.P. Morgan in October 2025 to raise €225 million in debt, which was secured via a private placement of bonds. The funds will be used to refinance the club’s existing loans and support day-to-day operations. “Our Global Credit Solutions Trading team works alongside our Banking, Public Finance and Private Bank partners to deliver bespoke financing and liquidity solutions, helping clubs and owners unlock value from player transfer-related cash flows, as well as media, sponsorship and other contractual receivables.” Global Head of Credit Solutions Trading, J.P. Morgan. Capital continues to pour into European football: according to Deloitte, club revenues are expected to hit a new record of €44 billion for the 2025/2026 season. However, the market is gradually maturing: alongside headline takeovers, a steady pipeline of refinancings and private placements is helping to create a deeper, more resilient investment ecosystem. J.P. Morgan has established an extensive track record across the full spectrum of European football finance, supporting some of the continent’s most prominent clubs — and this momentum looks set to continue. “There is an influx of new investors chasing sports and sports-related businesses as the market expands,” said Gian Piero Sammartano, global co-head of Sports Investment Banking at J.P. Morgan. “To this end, J.P. Morgan is committed to delivering holistic advisory and financing solutions to both current and prospective sports clients across the globe.” “J.P. Morgan is committed to delivering holistic advisory and financing solutions to both current and prospective sports clients across the globe.” Global Co-Head of Sports Investment Banking, J.P. Morgan JPM survey respondents identified financial market technology as traders’ primary market structure concern, ahead of liquidity. A recent report on the top 32 European clubs placed the total value at €72.6 billion, a 12% increase over 2025 and almost three times the level recorded when statistics were first aggregated in 2016.1 With those lofty valuations comes an increased level of competition, and an increasing concentration of value among the legacy clubs. In the English Premier League (EPL) alone, clubs paid a record €3.6 billion in transfer fees during the 2025 summer transfer window, according to data from transfermarkt.com.2 These fees are often settled through installments over several years, creating forecastable future cash inflows that can be converted into upfront funding from banks and private lenders. Monetizing these contractual receivables can provide clubs with a lower-cost way to raise working capital — financing that is increasingly necessary as player valuations rise and new regulations such as the EPL’s Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) cap allowable losses over a rolling multiyear period to promote financial stability. “European Football has evolved into an established institutional investment market, with a growing range of opportunities across the capital structure” says Taoufik Bounhar, global head of Credit Solutions Trading at J.P. Morgan. “Leading clubs have built globally recognized brands with significant commercial value. For alternative credit investors, that can translate into opportunities backed by newly contracted revenue streams that can be monetized or financed.” To harness this intrinsic brand value, raise working capital and remain competitive with peers, clubs are seeking innovative financing solutions to monetize their receivables into near-term liquidity. “We structure financing and asset monetization solutions around the clubs’ contractual cash flows, enabling them to accelerate liquidity, optimize their funding costs and manage balance-sheet counterparty exposures,” said Bounhar. Importantly, this financing format strives to be less about lending against team performance and more about converting unconditional cash flows into upfront liquidity. The purchase price is discounted at a rate tied to the buying club’s creditworthiness, the payment schedule and the available contractual and statutory protections. Across the seven major leagues, more than $1 billion in player transfer receivables have been transacted through J.P. Morgan over the past five years. In this arrangement, lenders monetize the receivables owed to a club under its commercial agreements, namely sponsorship, naming rights and kit supply agreements, helping the club raise liquidity. Credit assessment focuses on payment obligations, counterparty creditworthiness, remaining contract tenor, termination provisions and enforceability. Where contractual cash flows are sufficiently robust, the financing may be provided more efficiently than unsecured, club-level borrowing. In this arrangement, clients receive cash due from broadcaster deals, leveraging the credit quality of the broadcasters and high visibility of multi-year broadcasting cycles. Media rights financing is structured against identifiable broadcasting distributions or contracted payment entitlements. Advance rates, tenor and pricing depend on the certainty of those cash flows, the creditworthiness of the paying counterparty and exposure to sporting contingencies, including relegation. title: JP Morgan: investment surges and inflation bring volatility but family offices are enjoying the ride - Spear's Magazine
content:
The bank's family office co-head has said that 'many feel strongly that the risk of staying out is higher than the risk of getting in' Family offices are increasing their exposure to investment surges in AI and alternatives, appearing unphased by market volatility, according to analysis from JP Morgan. In London last week, JP Morgan held the launch of its Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions (LTCMAs). The annual briefing, now in its 31st year, is closely watched by the bank’s family office clients, and provides a 10 to 15-year forecast for risks and returns across various asset classes. At the briefing, Karen Ward, chief market strategist for EMEA at JP Morgan Asset Management, identified defence, energy and technology as three areas where government and private expenditure is surging: ‘The more chaotic the world becomes, the more this spending has to happen.’ [See also: Alternative assets now form the majority of family office portfolios] In the report, JP Morgan forecast total annual US AI capital expenditure to peak at $1.2 trillion in 2030, before declining each year after that, reaching just over $800 billion in 2040. ‘The markets are continually assessing whether it’s found a productive home for capital,’ Ward said, adding that technology creation ‘is the fun part’ for markets, whereas once that technology is deployed, ‘that learning process creates a lot of volatility.’ These large investment increases are changing how family offices are approaching portfolio selection, the bank has found. Public equities topped JP Morgan’s list of where family offices have put fresh capital in the last six months, with 81 per cent of those allocating more to equities naming AI as a priority investment theme. [See also: The best wealth managers for high-net-worth clients] John Bilton, head of strategic research, said inflation was also leading clients to rethink their portfolios, and allocate funds towards alternatives. ‘Alternatives are inflation-proof assets, and offer a good opportunity to diversify. I think manager selection has become more and more important,’ he said. Grace Peters, co-head of investment strategy at JP Morgan’s private bank, agreed: ‘The key notion is that there are greater opportunities to diversify, and greater rewards for doing so.’ [See also: J.P. Morgan: UHNWs should invest in security amid geopolitical tensions] Research by JP Morgan’s private bank found that almost half (43 per cent) of family offices have made fresh allocations to alternatives in the last six months. ‘This reflects a deliberate strategic shift, not routine rebalancing,’ the bank’s family office co-head Natacha Minniti commented of the findings. ‘Despite plenty of risk and noisy news flow, family offices have a risk-on attitude. If you look at their behaviour, investors have increased exposure in public and private equity. Many feel strongly that the risk of staying out is higher than the risk of getting in.’ Alluding to recent bond market unrest at this week’s briefing, Ward said lenders faced an ‘ugly beauty contest’ on who to issue debt to: ‘There is much more choice about who to allocate to, and so the bond market has the all-powerful role of having other options,’ she said, adding that southern Europe ‘is in a much more sustainable place’ than it has been for a while. title: Will JPMorgan's Nigeria Expansion Bolster Its Growth Prospects? - TradingView
content: JPMorgan Chase & Co. JPM is advancing its expansion plans in Nigeria after the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) granted approval-in-principle to establish JPMorgan Merchant Bank Nigeria Limited. The move marks a significant step in JPMorgan’s efforts to deepen its presence in Africa’s largest economy and expand its corporate and institutional banking services. Can JPMorgan’s Nigeria Banking License Strengthen Its African Presence? The CBN granted approval-in-principle to JPMorgan on Oct. 23, 2026, allowing it to proceed with plans to establish a merchant bank in Nigeria. The development follows the bank’s reported deposit of 50 billion Nigerian naira (approximately $38 million) with CBN as part of its licensing process. The deposit represented a key regulatory requirement but did not guarantee approval. JPMorgan Merchant Bank Nigeria Limited is expected to expand the bank’s ability to serve Nigerian corporations and institutional clients. Its proposed activities include wholesale banking, capital markets and advisory services. The expansion could also create opportunities in lending, payments, trade finance and cross-border transactions. JPMorgan has maintained a representative office in Lagos for years. Establishing a locally licensed merchant bank would provide a broader platform to serve businesses and participate in Nigeria’s financial markets. The approval-in-principle represents only the initial stage of the regulatory process. JPMorgan Merchant Bank Nigeria Limited must complete the remaining requirements, including incorporation with the Corporate Affairs Commission and the necessary operational arrangements, before receiving authorization to commence business. The proposed Nigerian merchant bank also aligns with JPMorgan’s broader efforts to strengthen its African presence and capture corporate and investment banking opportunities across the region. The bank has reinforced its regional investment banking leadership through appointments covering sub-Saharan Africa, Kenya and Ivory Coast, reflecting its focus on expanding client coverage and strengthening relationships with businesses, governments and institutional investors. Nigeria’s position as a major African economy could make the proposed bank a valuable addition to JPMorgan’s regional operations. However, the scale of the opportunity will depend on regulatory approvals, client demand and the bank’s ability to establish profitable operations. In conclusion, JPMorgan’s planned entry into Nigeria’s merchant banking sector could strengthen its African presence and create new growth opportunities in corporate banking, capital markets, advisory services and cross-border financing. Nigeria’s sizable economy and growing demand for institutional financial services offer significant long-term potential. However, the expansion’s success will depend on securing final regulatory approval, attracting corporate clients and building profitable operations amid competition and market challenges. While the approval-in-principle marks an important milestone, its contribution to JPMorgan’s overall growth will ultimately depend on how effectively the bank converts its expanded presence into sustainable revenue and earnings. The REIT will earn an asset management fee equaling 1.25% of Apollo’s equity, or $16.75 million, according to Executive Director Anthony Paolone. UDR’s $2 billion joint venture with Apollo got generally good reviews from Wall Street analysts after it was announced last week. Anthony Paolone, executive director at J.P. Morgan, called the JV “positive, in our view, and important, given that cap rates are likely 25bps or more higher today.” In the deal, Apollo-managed funds and affiliates will invest $1.34 billion of capital, acquiring an approximate two-thirds interest in the 19 properties that total 7,059 units. UDR, which will retain a one-third interest, will continue to operate and manage the portfolio and earn an asset management fee equaling 1.25% of Apollo’s equity, or $16.75 million, Paolone said in a research note. The deal seems to accomplish multiple goals for UDR, including lowering the average age of its portfolio, generating liquidity for new deals and stock buybacks and boosting fee-management returns. However, Apollo is a sophisticated operator and there are many unknowns, according to Paolone. In generating liquidity, UDR is trading out of older assets with the JV. The 19 properties, which carry a 6% cap rate, have average revenue per unit of $2,058 and an age of 39 years, per the release from UDR. By comparison, in the second quarter of 2026, UDR’s average rent was $2,642 for its 2Q26 same-store portfolio, Michael Lewis, an analyst for Truist, said in a report shared with Multifamily Dive. Removing the older assets enhances UDR’s “remaining same-store NOI growth rate,” Paolone wrote. The deal also shows that the jump in 10-year Treasury yields may be affecting valuations. “The quoted 6.0% cap rate appears to signal apartment cap rates may have moved up amid the recent spike in interest rates, though it is below the 6.4% implied cap rate on UDR’s stock,” Lewis wrote. Piper Sandler analyst Alexander Goldfarb concurred, writing that the valuations “are beginning to reflect the 5%-handle 10-Year,” with a 6% forward economic cap rate versus a net asset value cap rate of about 5%, he said in a report shared with Multifamily Dive. By comparison, Independence Realty Trust acquired Centerspace at 6.8%, which shows “the cash flow disconnect between the Midwest and Coastal/Sunbelt,” he wrote. Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Multifamily Dive free daily newsletter With the transaction, UDR will gain “access to a new, low-cost permanent source of equity capital,” CFO Dave Bragg said in the release. The REIT expects to deploy the proceeds into high-growth assets and other general corporate purposes. “The JV provides significant capital to improve/de-lever the balance sheet and pursue new investments,” Lewis said. Paolone said that UDR management expects to use the proceeds for acquisitions in the 5.25% to 5.5% cap rate range, debt paydowns and stock buybacks. He also noted that REITs in other sectors, like Realty Income in net lease, have tapped capital through JVs. “The fees and structure provide UDR with low-cost capital, though with some added complexity and some unknowns around the long-term features of the deal,” Paolone said. “It should be about 1% accretive to the bottom line, which is helpful in a low-growth area like multifamily right now.” Paolone said UDR’s management fee was “sizable” and set the deal apart. With a 6% cap, the $2 billion portfolio would generate about $120 million in net operating income. He said the venture appears to deduct $16.75 million in management fees, pay for capital expenditures and then make a distribution. With a modest capital ex of $10 million, the cash flow for partners would be $93.25 million, according to Paolone. Paolone projects Apollo to receive $62.5 million, or a 4.7% cash return on its investment, while UDR will earn $30.8 million in distributions plus its management fees for a total of $47.5 million. The REIT should be able to produce at least a 5.5% return, or $71.5 million. UDR’s total cash coming in from the deal should be $119 million, compared to $110 million from its wholly owned assets. “Our understanding of how these insurance company deals work is that each party receives pro rata distributions of cash flow,” Paolone wrote. At the fifth anniversary of closing, UDR will have the option to repurchase Apollo’s interest in the JV. While the deal looks like a winner for UDR, Paolone admitted there “could be devils in the details.” “Apollo is a sophisticated counterparty, and we find it hard to believe it is doing these deals in a manner that is completely favorable to the other party,” Paolone said. It’s also unclear what “downside support” UDR is providing to Apollo. “In the few deals we’ve seen REITs do with insurance companies, the finer points have not been disclosed,” he wrote. “This is something we’ll have to watch over time, and it does add complexity, of which we are not a fan.” Still, “on net” the deal looks good for UDR, according to Paolone. “It sheds lower-quality assets at a price level that seems to have been set a few months ago,” he wrote. “It will collect fees and add to earnings.  is the largest bank in the United States, and its quarterly report often sets the tone for the entire financial sector. This time the message was mixed but constructive. Revenue and net income rose from a year earlier, consumer banking delivered strong growth and the bank raised its interest income outlook. At the same time, earnings per share fell short of analyst expectations for the first time in several years, and the bank sharply reduced its share repurchases. Financial companies within the Russell 1000 have been navigating a new rate environment after the Federal Reserve's recent increase, and JPMorgan's results offered an early look at how that shift is playing out. Reported revenue rose compared with the prior year, and managed revenue, which adjusts for taxable-equivalent items, grew at a similar pace. Net income increased, and diluted earnings per share rose at a faster rate thanks to a lower share count. Excluding losses on discretionary investment securities, profit was higher still. Net interest income, the difference between what the bank earns on loans and pays on deposits, climbed at a double-digit rate. Excluding the Markets business, the increase was more modest but still solid, supported by higher deposit balances, growth in card balances and more wholesale lending. Noninterest revenue grew at a slower pace. The shortfall came mainly from capital markets. Fixed-income trading revenue declined from a year earlier, and management said client activity moderated during the quarter. Investment banking fees grew compared with last year but fell from the prior quarter. Equity trading, on the other hand, was strong and helped offset part of the weakness. Expenses also rose meaningfully, driven by compensation, marketing, brokerage-related and technology costs. Higher spending limited how much of the revenue growth translated into profit, which contributed to the gap versus estimates. Consumer and Community Banking was a bright spot. Revenue grew at a high single-digit rate, and net income rose at a double-digit pace. Card Services and Auto led the way, helped by higher card net interest income and auto lease income. Banking and Wealth Management also grew, supported by asset management fees and deposit balances. JPMorgan remained the largest retail deposit franchise in the country for another year and added a large number of net new checking accounts during the quarter. Client asset net inflows were substantial, reflecting continued trust in the bank's wealth platform. The most important forward-looking signal was an increase in the full-year net interest income forecast, both including and excluding Markets. The bank also gave a preliminary view for next year that points to further growth in net interest income excluding Markets. For a lender of JPMorgan's scale, interest income is the foundation of earnings. A higher outlook suggests that loan growth and deposit trends are strong enough to outweigh pressure from rate changes, at least for now. One of the most discussed details was capital return. Net share repurchases dropped sharply from the prior quarter, even as the bank continued to pay a sizeable common dividend. The standardized common equity tier one ratio also declined from a year earlier. Analysts have debated whether the slowdown reflects caution about the economic outlook, preparation for regulatory changes or a decision to keep capital available for lending and acquisitions. Whatever the reason, capital allocation is likely to remain a key question on future calls. The provision for credit losses was lower than a year ago, reflecting a smaller reserve build and lower net charge-offs. Stable credit is reassuring, especially after a rate increase that may eventually strain some borrowers. Higher interest rates can support lending margins, but they can also slow loan demand and raise default risk over time. Softer underwriting and bond trading activity may continue to weigh on investment banking revenue. Rising expenses are another area to watch, since technology and marketing investments are central to the bank's strategy. JPMorgan's wealth and asset management activities have become a growing source of stable fee income. Revenue in this area rose strongly, helped by higher market levels and strong net inflows from clients. Fee-based income is valuable for banks because it depends less on interest rate swings and loan demand than traditional lending. Payments are another quiet engine. Within the Commercial and Investment Bank, payments revenue and advisory work supported results even as bond trading slowed. Corporate clients rely on large banks for cash management, foreign exchange and transaction services, and these relationships tend to be sticky over many years. Taken together, lending, deposits, wealth and payments give JPMorgan a diversified earnings base. That diversification helps explain why the bank can absorb weakness in one business line without derailing overall profitability, a quality that many investors value in uncertain markets. Followers of Financial Stocks often use JPMorgan as a barometer for the industry. This quarter suggests that the core lending and deposit engine remains powerful, while capital markets activity is more sensitive to rate and economic uncertainty. Return on tangible common equity remained at a healthy level, showing that the franchise continues to generate strong profitability. Over the coming months, investors will watch whether loan growth persists, whether trading activity rebounds and how the bank balances dividends, share repurchases and capital buffers. The raised interest income outlook gives JPMorgan a firm base, but the pace of capital return will help shape sentiment toward the stock and the broader banking group into the new year. title: J.P. Morgan Projects a 7.0% Annual Return for a 60/40 Investment Portfolio over 10–15 Years - Funds Society
content: The projected annual return for a U.S. dollar-denominated 60/40 stock and bond portfolio over the next 10–15 years rises to 7.0%, although higher correlations between stocks and bonds call for additional diversification. This is the main takeaway from the 31st edition of the 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions (LTCMA) report by J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The study offers a comprehensive 10- to 15-year outlook on the future returns and risks across various investment asset classes, against a backdrop where inflation uncertainty and market volatility remain elevated. While labor and demographic headwinds may constrain long-term growth potential, the report argues that increased capital expenditure and the adoption of artificial intelligence across sectors will bolster near-term earnings and lift long-term productivity. The report emphasizes the potential of regional equity diversification and the inclusion of alternative assets, particularly hedge funds and real assets. A 60/40+ portfolio with a 30% allocation to diversified alternatives could boost expected returns up to 7.5% and improve the Sharpe ratio by 21% compared to a conventional 60/40 portfolio. “Our long-term capital market assumptions help investors navigate markets reshaped by economic nationalism, technological acceleration, and shifting capital flows. This year’s outlook points to stronger long-term growth and new opportunities to build more resilient portfolios through diversification—combining higher global fixed-income yields with alternative and real assets that deliver differentiated return sources and enhanced inflation protection,” noted John Bilton, Global Head of Multi-Asset Strategy at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. For his part, David Kelly, Chief Global Strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, commented: “The global economy is entering a dynamic investment cycle in which AI adoption and productivity gains reinforce growth prospects. At the same time, demographic challenges, elevated public deficits, and a more complex geopolitical landscape suggest that inflation will remain more volatile across our forecast horizon.” Regarding the report’s practical utility, Grace Peters, Global Co-Head of Investment Strategy at J.P. Morgan Private Bank, explained: “Each year, the assumptions from our LTCMA report provide the foundation for building client portfolios, and that has never been more critical than it is today. Returns matter, but they are no longer the only factor to consider. In the current environment, achieving an optimal balance between risk and return is essential. High market dispersion creates opportunities for investors who take a disciplined approach to strategic asset allocation, looking beyond what the headlines might suggest.” The firm explains that three core forces are shaping the future and will drive returns. The first is economic nationalism, which spurs state investment, though risks linked to inflation volatility persist. Second, technology adoption is underpinning the global economy by driving investment and productivity. Meanwhile, a surge in domestic investment is prompting a reallocation of capital and altering the dynamics of public and private flows. The best growth prospects for the developed world in 15 years: The report notes that a global investment boom focused on artificial intelligence, set to extend through 2040, will lift total factor productivity by 50% to 120 basis points. This boost raises the forecast for U.S. real GDP growth to 2.1% and developed-market nominal growth to 4.2%. In addition, the policy mix of GDP and inflation is the most favorable seen since the pandemic. Furthermore, upward revisions to U.S. equities, a global bond revival, and a maiden analysis of bitcoin take center stage. According to the study, profit margins exceeding 15% lift the forecast for U.S. large-cap equities by 80 basis points to 7.5%, leading developed market equity expectations to surpass emerging markets for the first time in the report’s history. Meanwhile, rising real yields push global aggregate bond forecasts up from a low of 2.1% in 2021 to 5.3% today—the highest level in two decades. The document also includes an expected return range for bitcoin, although the asset is not included as a portfolio allocation. Regarding alternative assets, they offer superior returns, enhanced diversification, and strengthened inflation protection. Higher inflation volatility, persistent currency debasement risks, and expanding alpha-generation opportunities reinforce the role of alternative assets as an indispensable portfolio component and return engine. The analysis lifts the outlook for diversified hedge funds by 140 basis points, supported by sustained alpha resilience and a higher interest-rate regime. Concurrently, it maintains a constructive outlook on real assets given their capacity to hedge against heightened inflation volatility. Intermediate-term U.S. Treasuries are expected to deliver a 4.6% return, supported by expectations of higher policy rates and the reconstitution of term premia, which brightens long-term return prospects. U.S. investment-grade corporate debt is projected to return 6.1%, while U.S. high-yield debt is forecast at 6.7%, with a fair value spread of 440 basis points, driven by improved credit quality among the index’s constituents. U.S. large-cap equities are expected to yield 7.5% (up from 6.7% previously), reflecting persistent technology adoption and productivity gains. Nevertheless, elevated starting valuations and concentration risk remain vital considerations. Globally, equities are projected to return 7.5% (in USD), with non-U.S. markets offering richer diversification potential and benefiting from a U.S. dollar depreciation that proceeds at a more measured pace. For emerging markets, the report projects equity returns of 7.1% (in USD)—a lower figure than the previous year, as AI tailwinds and capital expenditures (capex) normalize. Alternatives encompass several distinct categories: Private Equity: Projected return stands at 9.8%, marking a slight moderation. Return potential remains anchored to consistent value creation and operational efficiencies, including AI integration across portfolio companies. Real Estate: Core U.S. real estate is projected to return 8.1%, while European core real estate is set at 7.1%. Core Global Infrastructure: Forecast to deliver 7.1% (up from 6.5% last year), mirroring supply chain reconfigurations. Commodities: Broad-basket commodities return forecasts rise to 4.8%, as access to critical minerals remains constrained and geopolitical risks weigh on the outlook. Gold holds steady at 5.5%. Timberland: Global timberland assets are expected to generate 6.2%, slightly below the 6.3% recorded the previous year. Hedge Funds: Diversified hedge funds are projected to return 6.7%, up from 5.3% last year, reflecting higher alpha estimates. The Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions (LTCMA) report is the product of an exhaustive research process combining quantitative and qualitative inputs from more than 90 leading portfolio managers, economists, and research analysts globally. These time-tested projections cover over 200 assets denominated in more than 20 currencies, serving as a benchmark for strategic asset allocation and long-term investment planning across today’s evolving financial landscape.

title: Jamie Dimon Hated Bitcoin: JPMorgan Now Expects BTC to Beat Stocks and Gold - CryptoPotato
content: JPMorgan’s long-term CEO, Jamie Dimon, once called bitcoin a “fraud,” said that it was “worthless,” and described it as a “decentralized Ponzi scheme.” Moreover, he claimed that if he were using the government, he would shut it down. Fast-forward several years, and the banking behemoth he runs is putting traditional finance on public blockchains, accepting BTC and ETH as collateral, and, oh right, predicting that BTC could outperform stocks and gold over the next 10-15 years. One of the first criticisms caught on camera from Dimon dates back to at least 2017, when he called the largest cryptocurrency a “fraud” that would eventually blow up. He added that JPM traders caught dealing with it would be fired and also compared BTC to the infamous tulip bubble. Although he later regretted using the term “fraud,” his hostile stance continued. Four years later, Dimon advised investors to “stay away” from crypto, arguing that the asset class could not compare with fiat currencies or gold. He also described bitcoin as “worthless” and the “fool’s gold of the future.” By 2022, the rhetoric had become even stronger as Dimon described Bitcoin and other digital assets as “decentralized Ponzi schemes.” In 2023, he kept the blows coming, dismissing BTC as a “pet rock.” The same year saw perhaps the most memorable attack. During a Senate hearing, the exec said that if he were running the US government, he would “close it down,” while claiming that cryptocurrencies were heavily associated with criminal activity. Despite all of his criticism and blatant claims, JPMorgan’s business strategy was already moving in a very different direction. The bank launched JPM Coin, built its Onyx blockchain infrastructure, executed tokenized collateral transactions involving BlackRock and Barclays, invested in blockchain intelligence company TRM Labs, and gave wealth-management clients access to crypto funds. The divergence between Dimon’s public comments and JPM’s commercial strategy has become even harder to ignore. The Wall Street behemoth recently let institutional clients use BTC and ETH as collateral for loans, one of its most direct integrations of native crypto assets into conventional banking. It has also worked with Coinbase to make crypto purchases more accessible to Chase customers, while JPMorgan Securities has served as an authorized participant for BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin ETF. On the blockchain side, JPM has expanded into public networks, with JPM Coin (JPMD) now available on Ethereum and Base. The bank has also launched tokenized money-market funds on Ethereum and is expanding JPM Coin to the Canton Network. The winds seem to have shifted after its report last week. Although the bank still believes BTC could be highly volatile, it predicted that the leading cryptocurrency – once referred to as “fraud” and “worthless,” is likely to outperform large-cap stocks, REITs, and gold over the next 10-15 years with a 10% annual compounded return. JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM | JPM Price Prediction) has made headlines by placing nearly $900 million in tokenized funds on both Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL). A tokenized fund is an investment fund whose shares exist as tokens on a blockchain, allowing them to trade around the clock. According to Sentora data, the JPMorgan OnChain Liquidity-Token Money Market Fund (JLTXX) holds about $792 million across both networks, while the My OnChain Net Yield Fund (MONY) holds an estimated $103.1 million on Ethereum alone. In just one week, JPMorgan took two significant steps. On October 19, 2026, Kinexys, the bank’s blockchain unit, introduced its JPM Coin deposit token (JPMD) to Ethereum. Shortly after, on October 22, J.P. Morgan Asset Management launched MONY and JLTXX on Solana. However, despite these announcements, both cryptocurrencies saw declines: ETH fell to $2,333, down 2.1% for the week, while SOL dropped to $101, down 1.5%. JLTXX is a U.S.-registered government money market fund that invests cash in short-term government debt and passes interest earnings directly to investors. JPMorgan designed it so that stablecoin issuers can hold reserves in JLTXX tokens under the GENIUS Act, a federal stablecoin law. JPMorgan first launched JLTXX on Ethereum in May. MONY, by contrast, is a private placement regulated under the SEC’s Rule 506(c), meaning only high-net-worth individuals can invest. JPMorgan rolled this fund out in December 2025. Both funds operate through Morgan Money, JPMorgan’s cash management platform, allowing investors to subscribe and redeem, then receive tokens at a designated blockchain address. In 2017, he derided Bitcoin as a "fraud" heading toward a crash. He has kept up a barrage of criticism against Bitcoin, dismissing it as "a pet rock" and "worthless" over the years. Just last year, JPMorgan began allowing its clients to buy Bitcoin as banks developed a stronger interest in crypto. "I don't think you should smoke, but I defend your right to smoke," Dimon said during JPMorgan's annual investor day in May 2025. "I defend your right to buy bitcoin." However, the report offered a significant caveat for its projection: It still doesn't recommend Bitcoin as something that investors should purchase for a diversified portfolio. Bitcoin is a digital asset designed to be sent electronically between users anywhere in the world without a bank or government facilitating the transfer. Therefore, its value is not determined by a central government. It only stems from what an investor is prepared to pay. "We see bitcoin as a speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing." At its peak in October 2025, Bitcoin reached just over $126,000 in value. Bitcoin's volatility is reflected in JPMorgan's forecast projections. It laid out a base case for roughly 10% returns over the next decade. The firm's "bear case" showed it could plunge about 10% in the same time frame. If Bitcoin had an extraordinary run, the firm's "bull case" said it could grow 17% in the next 10 years. Still, its status as a purely speculative investment led JPMorgan's asset management arm to consult against acquiring it. title: JP Morgan receives preliminary approval to establish merchant bank in Nigeria — Premium Times Nigeria - UA.NEWS
content:
The Central Bank of Nigeria has granted JP Morgan approval in principle to establish JP Morgan Merchant Bank Nigeria Limited in the country. The institution plans to provide wholesale banking services, operate in capital markets, and offer advisory services. As Premium Times Nigeria reports, approval in principle is the first stage of licensing and does not mean that a final banking license has been obtained. Before starting operations, JP Morgan must still complete regulatory procedures, including registering with Nigeria’s Corporate Affairs Commission and obtaining operating permits. The bank has had a representative office in Nigeria for many years. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. The central bank also approved Adedapo Olagunju’s candidacy for the position of managing director of the future bank. Lattera Kevin George, Nzela Chinedum Izunwanne, and Said Gabriel Murtaza were approved as non-executive directors. Central Bank of Nigeria Governor Olayemi Cardoso said the regulator aims to build a stable, competitive, and internationally connected financial system capable of supporting investment and economic growth. Earlier, Bloomberg, citing informed sources, reported that JP Morgan had paid 50 billion naira — about $38 million — to the central bank. According to the agency, the bank expects to obtain a license by the end of the year or in early 2027 if it receives all necessary approvals.
